summary: This memo specifies a method for sending IP multicast datagrams over Token-Ring local area networks. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Token-Ring cannot give every IP multicast group its own hardware address. This RFC maps IP multicast to a shared functional address, so systems must inspect received frames to identify the IP traffic they need.

questions: how does multicast work on token ring
how does ip multicast work over token ring
what token-ring address is used for ip multicast
subtitle: Maps IP multicast traffic to Token-Ring hardware addresses using a shared functional address.

tldr.problem: Token-Ring has only 31 functional hardware addresses, too few to assign a distinct one to every IP multicast group.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends mapping all IP multicast addresses to one functional address and configuring hosts to examine received frames for relevant IP traffic.
tldr.outcome: Systems on a physical ring must agree on the mapping method. Unit metadata classifies RFC 1469 as Historic.

today: RFC 1469 is classified as Historic in the unit metadata. It specifies a way to map IP multicast datagrams onto Token-Ring local area networks.

sections.title: Why Token-Ring Needs a Shared Address
sections.content:
IP multicast sends datagrams to a group of hosts using destination addresses in the range 224.0.0.0 through 239.255.255.255. Network hardware also needs a way to identify multicast frames.

Token-Ring provides only 31 functional addresses, shared among network functions. That is too few for a separate hardware address for every IP multicast group.
sections.plainLanguage: IP multicast can address many groups, but Token-Ring has only a small set of functional hardware addresses. The groups therefore need to share an address.

sections.title: Token-Ring Functional Address
sections.content:
The RFC recommends mapping IP multicast addresses to the functional address 03-00-00-20-00-00 in canonical form, or C0-00-00-04-00-00 in the bit order used by Token-Ring interfaces.

Because other protocols may use the same functional address, a frame sent to it is not necessarily an IP multicast frame.
sections.plainLanguage: All IP multicast groups use the same Token-Ring functional address. Other protocols may share it, so the address alone does not identify the frame's contents.

sections.title: Selecting a Mapping Method
sections.content:
The RFC describes three possible mappings: the all-rings broadcast address, the assigned functional address, and existing IEEE-assigned IP multicast group addresses. Each physical ring must use an agreed method, and a network interface should be configurable.

Using existing IEEE group addresses is recommended when the hardware supports it. Otherwise, the assigned functional address is preferred over all-rings broadcast. Systems using the functional address must also support all-rings broadcast for backward compatibility.
sections.plainLanguage: Every system on a ring needs to use compatible address mapping. The RFC prefers more specific group addresses when hardware supports them and requires support for the older broadcast method in certain cases.

sections.title: Filtering Received Frames
sections.content:
Since the assigned functional address may be shared with other protocols, a host receiving frames at that address must determine whether a frame contains IP multicast traffic and whether it is relevant to its group memberships.

The RFC says bridges may translate between mapping methods used on different physical rings.
sections.plainLanguage: A host must inspect frames received at the shared address to decide which ones contain IP multicast traffic it needs. Bridges may translate between address methods on connected rings.
